profile.name: Pony
profile.tagline: A 1960s novelty dance mimicking a galloping horse to a rhythmic beat.
profile.insight: In 1961, Chubby Checker topped the US charts with 'Pony Time', popularising a craze where dancers mimicked riding a horse.
profile.profile: The Pony is a 1960s fad dance made famous by Chubby Checker's hit single 'Pony Time'. Dancers keep their feet comfortably close together while hopping or rhythmically stepping to a 1&2, 3&4 beat to emulate riding a horse. The dance is performed without touching, often by couples facing one another who may turn or move around the floor. It remained a staple of 1960s pop culture and was later revived by performers such as Cindy Wilson of The B-52's.
profile.profile_long:
Origins and History
The Pony dance style emerged in popular culture during the early 1960s, closely tied to the song 'Pony Time'. Originally written by Don Covay and John Berry and recorded in 1960 by Covay with his group the Goodtimers, the track reached widespread fame when recorded by Chubby Checker the following year. Checker's 1961 release became his second US No. 1 single and topped the R&B charts, propelling the accompanying horse-riding dance style into mainstream youth culture across North America.

How It Is Danced
When executing the Pony, dancers move to a rhythmic beat of 1&2, 3&4. The basic posture requires keeping the feet comfortably together while generating a rhythmic motion that imitates the look of riding a horse. Dancers do not touch; instead, couples generally face each other while executing various arm and hand motions. Although there is no fixed line-of-dance, participants can move around the dance floor, integrating turns and chase positions into their performance.

Music and Instruments
The dance is performed to rock and roll and R&B music driven by mid-tempo 1960s dance beats. Chubby Checker's 'Pony Time' features iconic vocal cues, including reversing the traditional equestrian commands 'gee' (right) and 'haw' (left). The rhythm relies on a prominent subdivided beat (1&2, 3&4) that dictates the footwork cadence.

Costume and Setting
While originally danced in informal pop settings and teen dance halls, the style became strongly linked with early 1960s visual aesthetic. Performers such as Cindy Wilson of The B-52's adopted early '60s-style outfits and hairstyles when performing the Pony in television appearances such as Saturday Night Live in 1980.

Occasions and Meaning
Created as a fun solo-in-partner social dance, the Pony allowed dancers to express individuality without formal physical contact. It was widely cited in mid-century and retro pop songs, including Wilson Pickett's 'Land of a Thousand Dances', Nick Lowe's 'I Knew the Bride', and The Go-Go's 'We Got the Beat', solidifying its place as a symbol of 1960s dance party culture.

sections.origins_and_history: The Pony was introduced as a dance style alongside the 1960 song 'Pony Time', written by Don Covay and John Berry. Chubby Checker's 1961 recording of the song became a US No. 1 hit and popularised the dance nationwide.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dancer attempts to look as if riding a horse. The beat is 1&2, 3&4. Dancers keep their feet comfortably together while executing arm and hand motions. Couples generally face each other without touching and may perform turns or chase positions while moving across the floor.
sections.music_and_instruments: Danced to 1960s R&B and rock and roll tracks featuring a 1&2, 3&4 beat rhythm. The lyrics of 'Pony Time' feature vocal commands such as 'gee' and 'haw'.
sections.costume_and_setting: Social dance halls and party settings. Later television and stage performances featured mid-century early 1960s outfits and hairstyles.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: A 1960s novelty party dance designed for open social dancing, youth gatherings, and rock and roll television showcases.
sections.notable_figures: Chubby Checker (who popularized 'Pony Time' in 1961), Don Covay and John Berry (songwriters), and Cindy Wilson of The B-52's (who performed the dance in 1978–1980).
sections.lineage: Emerged from American 1960s rock and roll fad dances following the popularity of the Twist.

basic_steps: Step or hop in place to the rhythmic count of 1&2, 3&4.
Imitate riding a horse using optional hand and arm motions.
Maintain a position facing your partner without physical contact.
Optionally add turns or chase movements around the dance space.
teaching.formation: Non-touching couples facing each other; open space with no line-of-dance.
teaching.level_notes: Accessible to beginners; focuses on rhythm and relaxed horse-riding imagery.

music_profile.vocal_style: Upbeat 1960s R&B/rock and roll vocals with rhythmic calls
music_profile.sound_description: Mid-tempo early 1960s rock and roll driving an accented 1&2, 3&4 beat rhythm, characterized by expressive vocals and rhythmic calls.

movement_profile.posture: Upright or slightly bent knee stance attempting to look as if riding a horse.
movement_profile.footwork: Feet kept comfortably together, moving on counts 1&2, 3&4.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Various arm and hand motions are possible, mimicking holding reins or rhythmic pumping.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Rhythmic bouncing motion corresponding to a horse-riding appearance.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Couples generally face each other without touching; open floor with no line-of-dance; turns and chase positions allowed.

signature_moves.name: Horse-riding bounce
signature_moves.description: Rhythmic bounce keeping feet together to look as if riding a horse on beat 1&2, 3&4.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Low bouncing off the balls of the feet; no high jumps.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid touching partner or sticking strictly to a rigid line-of-dance.

social_formats.description: Non-touching partner dance where couples face each other.

episode_brief.title_hook: Riding the 1960s Beat: The Pony Craze
episode_brief.logline: Discover how Chubby Checker turned an equestrian imitation into a national dance sensation in 1961.
beats: Show footage or recreation of Chubby Checker performing 'Pony Time' in 1961.
Break down the basic 1&2, 3&4 footwork and posture.
Demonstrate non-contact partner interaction and arm variations.
Explore how 1980s new wave acts like The B-52's brought the dance back into performance art.
Lead a group dancing the Pony freely across an open floor.

drills: Count 1&2, 3&4 aloud while bouncing softly on both feet.
Keep feet comfortably close together while maintaining rhythm.

lesson_ladder.goal: Add arm motions and non-touch partner facing position
drills: Add hand motions simulating holding reins.
Face a partner without touching while staying on beat.

lesson_ladder.goal: Execute turns and chase positions across the floor
drills: Perform full turns while keeping the 1&2, 3&4 bounce.
Move around partner in a chase formation.

visual_motifs: Couples facing each other on a dance floor without touching
episode_brief.instructor_persona: Upbeat, energetic documentary dance historian and instructor.
episode_brief.music_cue: Chubby Checker's 'Pony Time' playing at full volume.

connections.name: Twist
connections.note: Both were major early 1960s fad dances popularized by Chubby Checker recordings.

seniors.seated_version: Perform the 1&2, 3&4 rhythm seated in a chair, tapping feet comfortably together while moving arms gently.
seniors.standing_version: Stand near a chair for support, performing gentle low bounces on the spot.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Slower tempo with minimal foot elevation.

children.game_version: Pretend to be galloping ponies around an arena, keeping time with the 1&2, 3&4 beat.

gaps: Detailed formal footwork diagrams from 1960s instructional manuals are absent.

claims.text: Pony Time was written by Don Covay and John Berry and originally recorded in 1960 by Covay with the Goodtimers.
claims.quote: Pony Time is a song written by Don Covay and John Berry (a member of Covay's earlier vocal group, "the Rainbows"), and originally recorded in 1960 by Covay with his group "the Goodtimers".

claims.text: Chubby Checker's 1961 recording of Pony Time reached No. 1 on the US pop and R&B charts.
claims.quote: It achieved greater success when it was recorded by Chubby Checker the following year, becoming his second US No.1 (after his 1960 single "The Twist"). Chubby Checker's recording of "Pony Time" was also a No.1 hit on the R&B charts.

claims.text: The song introduced the Pony dance style in which the dancer looks as if riding a horse.
claims.quote: The song introduced a new dance style, the Pony, in which the dancer tries to look as if riding a horse.

claims.text: The beat of the Pony dance is 1&2, 3&4.
In the dance, feet are kept comfortably together while arm and hand motions are used.
claims.quote: In the dance the feet are kept comfortably together, while various arm and hand motions are possible.

claims.text: Couples generally face each other without touching, and there is no set line-of-dance.
claims.quote: Movement around the dance floor may occur, but there is no line-of-dance. Couples, who generally face each other, do not touch, and turns and chase positions are possible.

claims.text: Cindy Wilson of The B-52's performed the Pony in music video and TV appearances between 1978 and 1980.
claims.quote: Cindy Wilson of The B-52's can be seen performing the Pony in the video for their 1980 song, "Give Me Back My Man", as well as in other films of the band performing between 1978 and 1980 (including their 1980 appearance on Saturday Night Live).
